subtype: Approach: packing the finished work in the bag straight away [Action]
passage: Lerato wrote the last line of her homework and put down the pencil. She did not push the notebooks aside. She stacked the maths book and the reading book, slid them into her school bag, and zipped it closed by the door. Next morning in the flat in Johannesburg, her brother Thabo was tearing through his desk. "My worksheet! Where is it?" Lerato picked up her bag and put on her shoes. "Mine is already in the bag," she said. Thabo found his crumpled under a pile of papers just as the taxi hooted outside.

qa.q: Where did Lerato put her homework once it was finished?
qa.a: She put the notebooks in her school bag and zipped it closed by the door.

qa.q: What might Lerato have been feeling the next morning as Thabo searched for his worksheet?
qa.a: She was probably calm and quietly pleased. Her homework was already packed, so she only had to put on her shoes.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Thabo use to avoid the morning panic, and why?
qa.a: He could pack each finished sheet in his bag the same evening. Then the worksheet would be there when the taxi comes.

qa.q: How does Thabo see the morning after Lerato's calm answer?
qa.a: Thabo feels rushed and probably a little annoyed that his sister is ready. He finds the crumpled worksheet just in time.

grounding: A girl packs her finished notebooks into her school bag right away, which avoids the morning panic of hunting for homework on the study table.

subtype: Approach: counting days left and dividing the chapters [Thinking]
passage: On the way home from the village school, Seema walked with her classmate Deepika. "Four days until the Social Studies test," Seema said. She stopped and counted on her fingers. "Six chapters. Four days." She drew a chart in the dust with a stick. "Four into six. A chapter and a half each day." Deepika looked at the lines. "That's not so much." "No," said Seema. "It looked big before." At home she wrote it on the back of her notebook: Monday, chapters one and half of two. She tied a string around the page to mark it.

qa.q: How many chapters did Seema count for the test?
qa.a: She counted six chapters.

qa.q: What did Seema feel when she saw her plan was a chapter and a half each day?
qa.a: She felt relieved and more confident, since she said the work looked big before and now seemed smaller.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Seema use if she falls behind, and why?
qa.a: She could move the plan for the next day and add a short extra session. Small changes keep the plan working.

qa.q: How does Deepika see Seema's plan?
qa.a: Deepika sees the chart in the dust and thinks the work is not much. Deepika may feel less worried about the work too.

grounding: A child with a Social Studies test coming counts six chapters over four days and makes a plan for daily pieces, so the big task feels doable.

subtype: Approach: reading the chapter again and again [Action]
passage: In the school library, Karan opened his science chapter and read it once. Then he read it again, slowly, and a third time. He did not underline a single line. He nodded at each page. "I know this," he told himself. "It looks so familiar." He closed the book. Bhavna, a classmate at the next table, asked her own question: "Karan, what are the two kinds of mixtures in chapter four?" He looked at the ceiling and said, "It was on that page with the pictures." Then he opened the book and began the first page again.

qa.q: How many times did Karan read the science chapter?
qa.a: He read it three times.

qa.q: What was Karan feeling as he closed the book and said "I know this"?
qa.a: He felt sure and confident. The pages looked familiar, so he believed he was ready.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Karan try after Bhavna's question, and why?
qa.a: He could close the book and write down what he remembers from each page. Trying to recall shows what he really knows.

qa.q: How might Bhavna see Karan's answer to her question?
qa.a: Bhavna saw a classmate who could point to the page but not name the answer. She might wonder if he knew the chapter as well as he thought.

grounding: A boy rereads his science chapter three times and feels ready because the words look familiar, though he has only recognised the text and not tried to recall it.

subtype: Approach: feeling ready because the page looks familiar [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Jiya, and I closed my science book with a big smile. Photosynthesis, I had it. I had read the page four times and the picture of the leaf was in my head. At dinner Mummy put down her spoon and asked, "Beti, tell me how a plant makes its food." I opened my mouth. Sun. Leaf. Green. Then nothing came. "It takes light," I said, and stopped. My brother Arnab giggled. I felt my ears go hot. I had thought it was in my head. It was only that the page looked familiar. After dinner I opened the book again and tried to write the steps.

qa.q: What did Jiya's mother ask at dinner?
qa.a: She asked how a plant makes its food.

qa.q: What did Jiya feel when she could not explain the steps at dinner?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and surprised, since her ears went hot. She had believed she knew it.

qa.q: What could Jiya do differently to check her learning before dinner next time, and why?
qa.a: She could close the book and say the steps aloud to herself or a toy. She would find the gaps before anybody else asks.

qa.q: How might Arnab see Jiya's answer at dinner?
qa.a: Arnab finds it funny to see his sister go quiet, which is why he giggles. He may not realise it stung her.

grounding: A girl closes the book thinking she knows photosynthesis, but when her mother asks her to explain she cannot say the steps.

subtype: Approach: making questions and answering from memory [Thinking]
passage: Note from the Class 6 tutor, Thursday evening. Sahil sat with his science book and a pencil. Sahil made a question out of every heading. The one on seasons became, "Why is winter colder than summer?" Then he closed the book and answered aloud. "Because the earth is far from the sun?" He stopped, frowned and opened the book. "No. The tilt changes how the light falls." He ticked the right ones and put a cross by the wrong ones. Then he went back to read only the crossed topics. I did not tell him the answers. I only asked what he would study again. Himani, tutor

qa.q: What question did Sahil make from a heading?
qa.a: He asked, "Why is winter colder than summer?"

qa.q: What did Sahil feel when he stopped, frowned and checked the book after his first answer?
qa.a: He felt unsure and a bit puzzled, since he suspected his answer was wrong. Checking gave him the right idea.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Sahil use to check his answers, and why?
qa.a: He could ask a friend to ask the questions from the book. Hearing someone else's questions covers parts he may not think to ask.

qa.q: How does the tutor Himani see Sahil's method?
qa.a: Himani sees a boy who finds his own gaps and works on them, which is why Himani only asked what he would study again.

grounding: A boy turns each heading into a question and answers aloud with the book closed, and checking wrong answers tells him exactly what to study again.

subtype: Approach: teaching the chapter to a younger sibling or toy [Action]
passage: In the kitchen of their city flat, Pooja stood her little brother Rohan on a stool. "Today's lesson is the water cycle," she said. Her mother Madhuri held the kettle at arm's length, and steam rose from the spout. Pooja held a cold steel glass over the steam, at a safe distance. "See? The water goes up as steam, and touches something cold, and turns to drops." Tiny droplets covered the glass. "That's the cloud." Then she stopped. "And then the drops fall down as... um..." She frowned. "I need to read that part again."

qa.q: What did Pooja hold above the steam?
qa.a: She held a cold steel glass over the steam.

qa.q: What did Pooja feel when she stopped and said she needed to read that part again?
qa.a: She felt uncertain and a bit frustrated, because she noticed she could not explain what happens after the drops form.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Pooja use to learn the rest of the water cycle, and why?
qa.a: She could draw the cycle with arrows on a page. Drawing each step will show her which one is missing.

qa.q: How might Rohan see his sister's lesson?
qa.a: Rohan probably finds it exciting to watch the steam turn to drops on the glass. He may not notice where Pooja got stuck.

grounding: A girl explains the water cycle to her little brother with a steel glass and kettle steam held safely by her mother, and where she stumbles shows what she has not understood.

subtype: Approach: practising old test papers under time [Action]
passage: I'm Vikram, and last Sunday I sat down at our dining table and solved last year's maths paper. My sister Vinita put the clock in front of me and sat with her chin on her hand. "Start!" I got through the first questions quickly. Then question seven took me a long time. "Bhaiya, fifteen minutes on that one," Vinita said. I checked my answers with the answer sheet afterwards. I got most of the paper right, but I ran out of time at the end, and the last three questions were empty. I decided to skip any hard question, mark it, and come back to it if there was time left.

qa.q: Who put the clock in front of Vikram?
qa.a: His sister Vinita put the clock in front of him.

qa.q: What did Vikram feel when he saw the last three questions were empty?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and a bit annoyed with himself, since the time had gone on one hard question.

qa.q: What else could Vikram do to improve his timing, and why?
qa.a: He could decide how many minutes each question deserves before he begins. Then he will know when to move on.

qa.q: How does Vinita see Vikram's practice paper?
qa.a: Vinita sees a brother who lost time on one question, and she called out the minutes. She helped him notice it without giving answers.

grounding: A boy solves last year's maths paper with a clock, checks his answers and learns he spends too long on one question, so he decides to skip and return.

subtype: Approach: skipping the boring chapter and hoping it will not come [Pitfall]
passage: The night before the test, Rajni opened the Civics chapter and closed it again. "So boring," she told her friend Amandeep on the phone. "Ma'am never asks from it." "It might come," said Amandeep. "It won't," said Rajni. She spent the hour on the chapters she liked, and went to bed early. In the exam hall, the last page had a question worth eight marks. It was from Civics. She read it twice and wrote two lines, then stared at the clock. When the paper was returned, she had lost most of those marks, and they were the easy ones.

qa.q: How many marks was the Civics question worth?
qa.a: It was worth eight marks.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling when she saw the eight-mark Civics question?
qa.a: She felt shocked and uneasy. She read it twice, wrote only two lines and stared at the clock.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Rajni use for a chapter she dislikes, and why?
qa.a: She could read the chapter in short bursts, picking out the main points first. Then even a boring chapter would not leave big gaps.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see what happened in the exam?
qa.a: Amandeep warned Rajni that it might come, and it did. Amandeep may feel sorry for Rajni but also that the hint was ignored.

grounding: A girl skips the Civics chapter she dislikes and hopes it will not come, but the paper has an eight-mark question on it and she loses easy marks.

subtype: Approach: switching tactics after a bad practice score [Revision]
passage: Lavanya sat on the string cot outside her house in the village and made a quiz for herself, ten questions from her science chapter. She had read it twice. She scored five out of ten. She looked at the paper for a while. "Reading is not working," she said quietly. That evening her brother Ramesh saw her cutting a notebook page into small cards. On each she wrote a point on one side and a question on the other. She shuffled and tested herself. The next night she quizzed herself again and got eight right.

qa.q: What score did Lavanya get on her first quiz?
qa.a: She scored five out of ten.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel after looking at her score of five out of ten?
qa.a: She was disappointed but clear-headed. She quietly said reading was not working, which led her to change her method.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Lavanya add to her cards, and why?
qa.a: She could ask Ramesh to read her the questions. Answering out loud to someone else helps her practise saying it.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see Lavanya cutting the notebook page into cards?
qa.a: Ramesh sees his sister trying something new after a poor score, and he may be curious or proud. He notices her working hard on her own.

grounding: After scoring five out of ten on her own quiz, a girl notices reading alone is not working and switches to key-point cards she uses to quiz herself, and her next score rises.

subtype: Approach: studying with a friend and swapping questions [Action]
passage: After school in the small town, Hafsa and Shalini sat on the steps of the temple opposite the school gate, with their notebooks open. "Five questions each," said Hafsa. They wrote for ten minutes. Shalini wrote about the parts of a flower, and Hafsa wrote about seeds. Then they swapped papers. Hafsa answered fast. Shalini stopped at question four and said, "I don't remember the stigma." Hafsa explained it with a quick sketch, and Shalini nodded. When Shalini asked her about seeds, Hafsa found her own small gap, and they both laughed. They planned to swap again on Thursday.

qa.q: How many questions did each of them write?
qa.a: Each of them wrote five questions.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when she found her own small gap and laughed?
qa.a: She felt amused and at ease. She could laugh because it was an ordinary slip and her friend was there to fill it.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the two girls use if they have less time, and why?
qa.a: They could each write just two questions on the parts they find hardest. Fewer questions aimed at gaps make a short session useful.

qa.q: How does Shalini see Hafsa's sketch of the stigma?
qa.a: Shalini sees a clear explanation that fills the gap, and nods. It helped that a classmate explained it in a way Shalini could see.

grounding: Two classmates each write five questions for the other on different parts of the chapter, and hearing each other's explanations fills small gaps.
